obtained.how: Fisheries and Oceans Canada's own library copy (DFO Library, waves-vagues.dfo-mpo.gc.ca)

bibliography.checked_against: the title page (p. 1) and the report's 'correct citation' (PDF p. 4)
bibliography.note: Jordan, C., Backe, N., Wright, M.C. and Tovey, C.P. 2009. Biological synopsis of pumpkinseed (Lepomis gibbosus). Can. Manuscr. Rep. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 2886: iv + 16 p. (DFO Science Branch, Pacific Region, Nanaimo).

claims.claim: fecundity 1,500–7,000 eggs (Holtan 1998, via Jordan et al. 2009)
claims.quote: The female releases between 1 500 and 7 000 eggs in an irregular pattern
claims.conditions: eggs released by a female in a nest (one spawning); females may spawn in more than one nest; general account, no place or sample size
claims.note: This is eggs per spawning act as Jordan et al. cite Holtan (1998), not total annual fecundity; the Ontario LHD figure beside it (2,451–10,633) is a different quantity. The same paragraph gives 1,500–15,000 fry per nest (mean 8,000), also from Holtan 1998.

claims.quote: Eggs hatch three to five days after fertilization, depending on water temperature
claims.note: The sentence carries no citation of its own; the next sentence cites Holtan (1998), so 'Holtan 1998 via Jordan' is a fair reading.

claims.claim: colonial nests < 1 m deep on sand or gravel
claims.quote: small, circular nests on sand or gravel in water less than 1 m deep
claims.conditions: colonies of up to 15 nests; nests 10–38 cm across (Holtan 1998)
claims.note: In Jordan et al. this is cited to McPhail (2007), not Holtan; the row also cites the Ontario LHD, which may be its real source here.

claims.quote: Males then begin cleaning the nest for a second spawn
claims.conditions: after the young leave the nest; males may also spawn more than once with the same or different partners (Breder & Rosen 1966)
claims.note: Jordan et al. cite Scott & Crossman (1973) for this.

notes: Two values in the same Table 3.6-1 row, attributed there to other sources, differ from this synopsis: Jordan et al. put spawning at 15–25 °C (McPhail 2007), continuing into August up to 27.8 °C (Scott & Crossman 1973), against the row's 17–26 °C; and they say the larvae leave the nest 'around 10 to 11 days after hatching' (Scott & Crossman 1973; Rios-Cardenas 2005), i.e. about 13–16 d after spawning with 3–5 d incubation, against the row's '8–11 d after spawning'. Other values: maximum age 8–10 yr; up to 5 cm in the first year; maturity in the 2nd–3rd year (Scott & Crossman 1973); mature fish 13–20 cm, 0.23–0.34 kg (Holtan 1998); optimum temperature 24–32 °C; affected at pH 5.2–5.3 (Sun & Harvey 1986); young 3.5–14 mm TL school in littoral and limnetic zones. Holtan (1998) is a 6-page Wisconsin DNR Bureau of Fisheries Management species leaflet (reference list, p. 13), so the egg and fry numbers are a state agency's general figures, with no study site or sample size.
